messages.subject: Observe?
parts:
Hi all,

I was wondering if there were any examples of using observe?

I'm having an issue with reactiveUI based input variables not properly updating back to other reactive functions and I thought I could get around it with something like this:

traitrevise <- observe(function () {
  traitvalue <- input$trait
  
})

using traitvalue in place of input$trait in my reactive functions, but I'm getting this error: "Error in func() : object 'input' not found"

I'm not fully grasping the use of observe from the man page alone and thought seeing it in action would help.

Thanks!

Jared

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Observe?
parts:
I don't know if observe is going to help you here... would it be possible to show more of your server.R that is having the problem?

But to answer your question:

Reactive functions know when their results become out-of-date, and they notify any other reactive functions that are depending on those now-outdated results. But they don't actually re-execute themselves until the next time they are called. This is because the changes that have occurred might mean that this reactive function's calculations might not even be needed anymore. Shiny assumes that a reactive function in and of itself is not useful; it's only given usefulness when called by another reactive function.

If that was the end of the story, then no reactive function would ever get called; something is needed to kick off the entire chain of events. That's what "observe" does; it tells Shiny: this code needs to actually re-execute when it becomes outdated. Again, this is in contrast to reactive functions which tell Shiny: this code needs to notify its dependencies when it becomes outdated, but don't actually re-execute it until someone calls it. In other words, reactive functions are lazily evaluated while observers are eagerly evaluated.

99.9% of the time you won't need to use observe directly, because reactive outputs use observe under the hood. So when you say this:

output$myPlot <- reactivePlot(function() { plot(get(input$dataset)) })

what's really happening is something like this:

myPlot <- reactive(plotWrapper(function() { plot(get(input$dataset)) }))
observe(function() {
  sendOutputToBrowser("myPlot", myPlot())
})

So the only reason you would need to use observe directly is if you have some reactive code you want to get called that has nothing to do with Shiny outputs.

I need to do a series of blog posts about the reactive programming features of Shiny, I know our current documentation glosses over the subject a little bit.

messages.subject: Re: Observe?
parts:
Hi Joe,

Thank you for the explanation. I found another solution. It seemed that shiny would get stuck when it tried to build a list with non-existant data and stop trying to update the list, even after the other reactive functions kicked in and the data was available. What I did was just put in some if() statement to stop problematic statements from executing until the data got there, for example:

output$cropstates <- reactiveUI(function() {
  stateselect <- as.list(levels(droplevels(traits[traits$crop==input$crop,"state"])))
  names(stateselect) <-levels(droplevels(traits[traits$crop==input$crop,"state"]))
  selectInput("state", "State:",
            stateselect)
  
})

output$croptraits <- reactiveUI(function() {
  if (length(levels(droplevels(traits[traits$state==input$state&traits$crop==input$crop,"trait"])))==0) {
    h4("Loading...")
  }
  else {
    if (input$alltraits=="all") {
      traitlabel <- "Sort by Trait:"}
    else if (input$alltraits=="indiv") {
      traitlabel <- "Choose Trait:"}
      traitsselect <- as.list(traits[traits$state==input$state&traits$crop==input$crop,"trait"]) 
      names(traitsselect) <- traits[traits$state==input$state&traits$crop==input$crop,"traitname"]
      selectInput("trait", traitlabel,
                  traitsselect)
  }
})

In the above example (not very elegant code I know), not all crops in all states have data, and I needed to give output$cropstates time to rebuild the list of available states. Before I put the if() statement into output$croptraits, the function would get hung up with the lack of a list in traitselect. The problem then became that even thought the other reactive functions would ultimately revise, the value of input$state would get stuck and I would have to refresh the webpage to clear it...

Thanks,

Jared

messages.author: 2935e7de556025cb
messages.subject: Re: Observe?
parts:
Hi Joe,

The reason that I put the "state" selectInput in a reactiveUIs is that not all state / crop combinations have trait data. The variable "traits" is basically an incidence data.frame stored in global.R. When someone selects a specific crop, that will limit which states are listed in the selectInput. When they selected a specific crop and state, that determines the traits they can see. 

Again, I'm sure that someone else could build this more elegantly. I really appreciate all your input.

Jared
